blurb: The Buddha's path out of suffering, carried by monks, merchants, and kings from India across all of Asia — and, in the last century, to the West.

events.description: Siddhartha Gautama renounces palace life, awakens under the Bodhi tree, and teaches the Four Noble Truths and the Eightfold Path. Traditional dates (563–483 BCE) are later than most modern scholarly estimates (c. 480–400 BCE).
events.title: Life of the Buddha

events.description: After the Buddha's death, councils at Rajagriha and Vesali (by traditional account) rehearse and preserve his teachings orally as the monastic community — the sangha — grows and begins to differentiate.
events.title: Councils & the early sangha

events.description: The Mauryan emperor Ashoka, remorseful after conquering Kalinga, patronizes Buddhism, carves edicts on dhamma across his empire, and — by tradition — sends missions as far as Sri Lanka and the Hellenistic world.
events.title: Ashoka spreads Buddhism

events.description: In Sri Lanka, the orally preserved Tipitaka is committed to writing (traditionally at Aluvihare, 29–17 BCE) — the textual basis of Theravada Buddhism.
events.title: The Pali Canon written down

events.description: New sutras — the Perfection of Wisdom among them — exalt the bodhisattva ideal and the emptiness of all phenomena, opening the 'Great Vehicle' (Mahayana) alongside the older schools.
events.title: Mahayana sutras composed

events.description: Carried by merchants and translator-monks such as Kumarajiva, Buddhism enters China (traditionally in 67 CE) and is gradually sinicized over the following centuries.
events.title: Buddhism travels the Silk Road to China

events.description: Nagarjuna argues that all phenomena are empty of independent essence (sunyata) — the Middle Way philosophy that shapes Mahayana thought from Tibet to Japan.
events.title: Nagarjuna & Madhyamaka philosophy

events.description: Around the semi-legendary Bodhidharma and later masters such as Huineng, Chan emphasizes direct insight and meditation over scripture — the seed of Zen in Korea and Japan.
events.title: Chan (Zen) Buddhism forms in China

events.description: Under the Tibetan empire, Buddhism is adopted from India — Samye monastery is founded c. 779 — blending Mahayana philosophy with tantric practice into what becomes Vajrayana.
events.title: Buddhism established in Tibet

events.description: Tradition dates Buddhism's official introduction to Japan — a gift of sutras and a Buddha image from the Korean kingdom of Baekje — to 552 CE (some sources say 538).
events.title: Buddhism reaches Japan

events.description: Through Sri Lankan monastic lineages, Theravada Buddhism becomes the majority tradition of Burma, Thailand, Laos, and Cambodia.
events.title: Theravada becomes dominant in Southeast Asia

events.description: From the 1893 World's Parliament of Religions, through Zen's literary vogue and the Tibetan diaspora after 1959, Buddhism — and its meditation practices — takes root in Europe and the Americas.
events.title: Buddhism reaches the West

name: Buddhism
